This module is arguably the most foundational part of your entire research project. Before speculative execution, before verification, before scheduling, there is one fundamental question:

> **What exactly should one AI agent transmit to another so that the receiving agent can continue computation as efficiently as possible?**

Today, the answer is almost always **natural language**. This module investigates whether that answer is fundamentally suboptimal.

---

# The Fundamental Problem

Imagine two human programmers.

Programmer A spends three hours understanding a codebase.

When Programmer B asks what was learned, A writes:

> "The authentication system validates JWT tokens before checking the session store..."

Natural language is perfect because humans understand language.

Now replace the humans with LLMs.

Agent A spends thousands of forward-pass operations constructing an internal computational representation.

But instead of sending that representation...

it converts everything into English.

Then...

Agent B reads English...

and reconstructs another internal representation.

The pipeline becomes:

```text
Internal Representation
        │
        ▼
Natural Language
        │
        ▼
Tokenizer
        │
        ▼
Tokens
        │
        ▼
Transformer
        │
        ▼
Internal Representation
```

Notice something.

The actual information both agents need is only the **internal representation**.

Everything else exists because humans need to understand it.

---

# Why This May Be Wasteful

Suppose Agent A internally knows

```text
Goal:
Find papers on speculative decoding.

Relevant papers:
Paper 12
Paper 31
Paper 89

Confidence:
0.92

Reasoning graph:
...
```

Instead of transmitting

```text
{
 goal:23,
 paper_ids:[12,31,89],
 confidence:.92
}
```

it currently writes

> "I searched for speculative decoding papers and found three promising papers..."

The second agent then converts this paragraph back into vectors.

That means

```text
Vectors

↓

Words

↓

Tokens

↓

Vectors
```

Every conversion consumes

* inference
* compute
* latency
* tokens

without creating new knowledge.

---

# The Information Theory Perspective

Information theory separates

**Information**

from

**Encoding**

English is only one encoding.

JSON is another.

Graphs are another.

Binary is another.

Embeddings are another.

The information remains identical.

Example

These all represent the same knowledge.

Natural language

```text
Paris is the capital of France.
```

JSON

```json
{
 city:"Paris",
 relation:"capital_of",
 country:"France"
}
```

Knowledge graph

```text
Paris
  │
capital_of
  │
France
```

Embedding

```
[-0.22,0.87,...]
```

Different encodings.

Same semantics.

This module asks

> Which encoding is best **for machines**?

---

# What Happens Inside an LLM

People often imagine an LLM thinking in English.

It doesn't.

Internally

```text
Token

↓

Embedding

↓

Hidden States

↓

Attention

↓

MLP

↓

Hidden States

↓

Output Distribution
```

There are never English sentences inside.

Only very high-dimensional vectors.

Natural language only appears

* at the input
* at the output

Everything between is numerical computation.

---

# The Current Agent Pipeline

Most modern multi-agent systems look something like

```text
Agent A

↓

LLM

↓

Natural Language

↓

Prompt

↓

LLM

↓

Agent B
```

Notice that every communication requires

* prompt formatting
* tokenization
* inference
* decoding

again.

This is surprisingly expensive.

---

# What This Module Wants

Instead of

```text
Agent A

↓

English

↓

Agent B
```

we investigate

```text
Agent A

↓

Machine Representation

↓

Agent B
```

That representation could be

```text
Graph

Embedding

Typed Object

Latent Vector

IR

State Object

Execution Graph

Memory Object

...
```

The research question is

**Which representation minimizes computational overhead while preserving enough information for downstream computation?**

---

# Why "State" Matters

Suppose Agent A has already completed

* retrieval
* planning
* reasoning

Why should Agent B redo all that work?

Maybe Agent B only needs

```text
Current Goal

Completed Work

Remaining Tasks

Retrieved Facts

Confidence

Dependencies
```

instead of

a 5,000-token explanation.

That collection is what we currently call the **agent state**.

But we don't yet know its optimal form.

---

# The Difference Between Data and State

This distinction is crucial.

Data

```text
Paper.pdf
```

State

```text
Current task:
Summarize Paper.pdf

Completed:
Abstract
Introduction

Remaining:
Methods

Confidence:
0.81

Current hypothesis:
Speculative execution improves latency.
```

State contains computational progress.

Data contains raw information.

Speculative execution cares much more about state than raw data.

---

# This Looks Similar to CPU Architectures

Modern CPUs don't communicate using English.

One stage doesn't tell another

> "Please multiply register three by register four."

Instead

```text
Opcode

Destination Register

Source Registers

Flags

Program Counter
```

Everything is structured.

Efficient.

Minimal.

Machine-oriented.

Your research asks

> Can AI systems evolve from human-oriented communication to machine-oriented communication in the same way?

---

# A More General View: Machine-Oriented Communication

This module is not really about "removing English."

It is about designing an **Application Binary Interface (ABI)** or **Intermediate Representation (IR)** for intelligent agents.

Compilers already solved a similar problem.

High-level languages (Python, C++) are translated into IRs such as LLVM IR because machine-oriented representations are easier to optimize, analyze, and execute.

Your hypothesis is that agent systems may benefit from an analogous "Agent IR" that is optimized for inter-agent communication rather than human readability.

---

# Candidate Representations

At this stage, we should remain agnostic. Promising categories include:

| Representation              | Strengths                            | Weaknesses                                     |
| --------------------------- | ------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------- |
| Natural language            | Flexible, expressive, human-readable | High token cost, ambiguous, expensive to parse |
| JSON / Typed Objects        | Explicit schema, easy to validate    | Can become verbose for complex reasoning       |
| Knowledge Graphs            | Preserve relationships well          | Harder to serialize and evolve dynamically     |
| Embeddings / Latent Vectors | Compact, continuous representations  | Difficult to interpret and verify              |
| Execution Graphs            | Capture workflow dependencies        | May not encode semantic meaning alone          |
| Hybrid Representations      | Combine complementary strengths      | Increased system complexity                    |

A key goal of the module is to determine, through evidence, which representation (or combination) best supports agent collaboration.

---

# How This Fits Into the Larger Project

This module is **not** the speculative execution system itself. It provides the communication substrate that later modules will rely on.

```text
                 User
                   │
                   ▼
          Master Execution Agent
                   │
        ┌──────────┴──────────┐
        ▼                     ▼
 Speculative Agent      Speculative Agent
        │                     │
        └────── Machine Communication ──────┐
                                            ▼
                                  Verification Module
                                            ▼
                                      Commit/Rollback
```

Without an efficient communication mechanism, speculative execution may spend a significant portion of its time exchanging and reconstructing context rather than performing useful work.

---

# The Core Research Question

I would frame this module around a single, technically precise question:

> **What is the minimal machine-oriented representation of an agent's computational state that allows another agent to continue execution with equal or better performance than communication through natural language?**

That question is measurable, falsifiable, and broad enough to encompass symbolic methods (graphs, typed objects), neural methods (latent vectors, learned protocols), and hybrid approaches. It also aligns naturally with the later phases of your project: once such a representation exists, it becomes the substrate for speculative execution, verification, confidence estimation, and scheduling.

# Semantic State Communication Research Methodology

> **Purpose:** This document defines the research methodology used throughout the Semantic State Communication project. Rather than beginning with implementation, the project follows a rigorous research-driven workflow where every architectural decision is supported by literature, experimentation, and benchmarking.

---

# Research Philosophy

This project does **not** begin by attempting to invent a new communication protocol.

Instead, it follows the scientific method:

1. Understand the current state of the field.
2. Reproduce existing work.
3. Benchmark existing approaches.
4. Identify research gaps.
5. Develop new methods.
6. Benchmark new methods against existing systems.
7. Integrate validated findings into the larger speculative execution architecture.

The goal is not to prove that a particular communication protocol is superior.

The goal is to discover which communication protocols perform best under different conditions and whether a novel approach can improve upon the current state of the art.

```text
Literature Survey

```

# Stage 1 — Literature Survey

The project begins with a comprehensive review of existing research.

The objective is to understand:

- Existing communication protocols
- Current state-of-the-art approaches
- Strengths and weaknesses
- Existing benchmarks
- Existing implementations
- Research gaps

# Stage 2 — Paper Analysis

- Problem addressed
- Motivation

- Experimental methodology
- Evaluation metrics
- Strengths
- Weaknesses
- Relevance to this project

Every paper is documented within the project's Literature Database.

---

# Stage 3 — Implementation of Existing Methods

Before proposing new communication protocols, representative methods from the literature will be implemented.

Examples include:

- Natural Language Communication
- JSON-Based Communication
- Typed Object Communication
- Knowledge Graph Communication
- Embedding-Based Communication
- Latent Communication
- Hybrid Communication

The objective is not innovation.

The objective is to reproduce existing systems under a common experimental framework.

---

# Stage 4 — Benchmark Existing Methods

All reproduced systems will be evaluated using identical benchmark tasks.

Evaluation metrics may include:

## Performance

- End-to-end latency
- Communication latency
- Parallel execution efficiency

## Computational Cost

- Prompt token usage
- Completion token usage
- Total token consumption
- GPU computation time
- CPU computation time
- Memory usage

## Communication Efficiency

- Serialized message size
- Number of communication rounds
- Compression ratio
- Context growth

## Task Quality

- Task completion accuracy
- Information preservation
- Reasoning consistency
- Verification success
- Robustness

Using identical benchmark conditions ensures fair comparison between competing approaches.

---

# Stage 5 — Comparative Analysis

The benchmark results are analyzed to understand the trade-offs between existing communication methods.

Questions include:

- Which method minimizes latency?
- Which method minimizes token usage?
- Which method scales best?
- Which method preserves information most effectively?
- Which method is easiest to verify?
- Which methods are better suited for speculative execution?

The objective is understanding, not ranking.

Different communication methods may perform better under different workloads.

---

# Stage 6 — Research Gap Identification

Only after existing approaches have been thoroughly evaluated will new research directions be explored.

Research gaps may include:

- High communication overhead
- Excessive token consumption
- Information loss
- Poor scalability
- Difficult verification
- Inefficient serialization
- Redundant context transmission

The identified limitations become the motivation for novel communication protocols.

---

# Stage 7 — Novel Communication Design

New communication methods are designed specifically to address the limitations discovered during benchmarking.

Potential research directions include:

- Semantic State Communication
- State Difference Communication
- Graph Patch Communication
- Hierarchical State Transfer
- Confidence-Aware Communication
- Execution-Aware Communication
- Predictive Communication
- Hybrid Symbolic-Neural Communication

Every proposed method remains a hypothesis until experimentally validated.

---

# Stage 8 — Prototype Implementation

Each proposed communication protocol will be implemented within the common benchmarking framework.

The implementation should remain modular so that communication protocols can be exchanged without modifying the surrounding agent architecture.

This ensures fair comparison across all methods.

---

# Stage 9 — Comparative Benchmarking

Every newly proposed communication protocol will be evaluated against the previously reproduced baseline systems.

Evaluation will use the same benchmark suite developed during Stage 4.

This allows direct comparison between:

- Existing literature
- Newly proposed communication methods

Performance improvements must be demonstrated through quantitative evidence rather than intuition.

---

# Stage 10 — Integration

Once sufficient evidence has been collected, the most effective communication protocol(s) will become the communication layer used within the larger Speculative Agent Execution architecture.

Future research modules—including:

- Agent State Representation
- Verification
- Confidence Estimation
- Speculative Scheduling
- Commit/Rollback

will build upon the validated communication framework.

---

# Research Principles

The following principles apply throughout the project.

## Evidence Before Architecture

Architectural decisions should be supported by:

- Published literature
- Experimental evidence
- Reproducible benchmarks
- Clearly identified hypotheses

---

## Reproducibility

Every implementation should be reproducible.

Benchmark configurations, datasets, software versions, and experimental settings should be documented whenever appropriate.

---

## Fair Comparison

Existing and proposed communication methods should always be evaluated under identical benchmark conditions.

---

## Innovation Through Understanding

Novel communication protocols should only be developed after thoroughly understanding the strengths and limitations of existing research.

---

## Benchmark-Driven Development

Claims of improvement should be supported through quantitative evaluation rather than subjective observation.

---

## Continuous Documentation

Every completed research session should update the project's documentation, including:

- Literature Database
- Research Log
- Open Questions
- Project Context
- System Architecture

This ensures that the project's understanding evolves alongside its implementation.

---

# Expected Deliverables

By the completion of this module, the project should produce:

- A comprehensive literature survey of machine-oriented agent communication.
- Detailed analyses of representative research papers.
- Reproducible implementations of existing communication methods.
- A standardized benchmark for evaluating inter-agent communication.
- Quantitative comparisons across existing approaches.
- One or more novel communication protocols addressing identified research gaps.
- Experimental evaluation comparing proposed methods against the current state of the art.
- A validated communication subsystem ready for integration into the broader Speculative Agent Execution architecture.

---

# Guiding Principle

> **We are not attempting to prove that Semantic State Communication is superior.**

> **We are attempting to determine, through rigorous research and experimentation, whether machine-oriented communication can outperform traditional natural-language communication for collaborative AI systems, and if so, under what conditions.**

Every literature review, implementation, benchmark, success, and failure contributes toward answering that question.

1. **No standard benchmark suite exists yet for cross-paradigm comparison.** Every paper above benchmarks its own method against natural language, but almost none benchmark latent-vector methods against structured-symbolic methods against each other under identical tasks/models. 3. **Heterogeneous-model communication is barely explored.** Interlat tests cross-model latent transfer, but general symbolic/hybrid representations that work across different model families/vendors (which matters more in practice, since real deployments mix models) are underexplored.
4. **Confidence-aware and execution-aware state representations** (your Stage 7 list) are mentioned as future directions in multiple papers but rarely implemented end-to-end with a scheduler that acts on the confidence signal.

## 3. Feasibility assessment

- **Structured/symbolic track (JSON, typed objects, graphs):** fully feasible at your scale (student project, no special hardware). You can implement this with prompt-engineering + schema validation, no model access needed. Low risk, low compute cost.

- The CPU-ISA analogy is evocative but slightly misleading: CPU stages share a *fixed, hand-designed* ISA because correctness is provable and the state space is small. While natural language is the de facto communication medium for LLM-based agents, it presents a fundamental constraint. The process of downsampling rich, internal latent states into discrete tokens inherently limits the depth and nuance of information that can be transmitted, thereby hindering collaborative problem-solving. Inspired by human ''mind-reading'', we propose Interlat (Inter-agent Latent Space Communication), a paradigm that leverages the last hidden states of an LLM as a representation of its mind for direct communication (termed ''latent communication''). 

An additional compression process further compresses latent communication via entirely latent space reasoning. Experiments demonstrate that Interlat outperforms both fine-tuned chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting and single-agent baselines, promoting more exploratory behavior and enabling genuine utilization of latent information.

However, although readable by human, natural language introduces constrains on a model’s expressive range and can also impose redundant computation: LLMs must down-sample their rich, high-dimensional internal states into discrete tokens, typically exposing only a single linear thought in their message, i.e., a chain of thought (CoT) (wei2022chain) plan to advise another agent (yu2024natural). Furthermore, a large portion of the generated text serves to maintain linguistic coherence rather than to convey essential information (zhang2024cut). 

This inefficient paradigm results in ambiguous, lossy inter-agent communication that prevents effective coordination (chen2025reasoning), which remains a primary cause of task failures in multi-agent systems (cemri2025multi). Human communication, by contrast, is not limited to explicit language; much of it is implicit and nonverbal latent communication (bodycues; kelly2010two).

In multi-agent settings, we propose that latent communication provides an analogous form of human mind-reading: instead of inferring others’ thoughts from words, agents transmit representations that can display their latent thoughts for downstream use, enabling tighter alignment of intentions. What happens when AI agents stop talking to each other — and start sharing thoughts directly?

LatentMAS introduces a revolutionary training-free framework enabling LLM-based multi-agent systems to collaborate purely through continuous latent representations rather than text, achieving 14.6% higher accuracy, 83.7% fewer tokens, and 4.3× faster inference across reasoning, commonsense, and coding benchmarks without any additional training. Imagine a team of expert consultants working on a complex problem. In today’s multi-agent AI systems, these “consultants” — individual large language models — must communicate every thought, every reasoning step, and every intermediate conclusion through text. 

It’s as if our consultants were forced to write formal memos for every single idea before passing it to their colleagues. This is precisely how modern LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) operate. From mathematical reasoning pipelines to code generation frameworks, agents coordinate through natural language — what researchers call the lingua franca of AI collaboration .

content.title: When Less Latent Leads to Better Relay: Information-Preserving Compression for Latent Multi-Agent LLM Collaboration
content.text:
## 1 Introduction

Large language model (LLM) based multi-agent systems rely on communication to coordinate reasoning, critique intermediate outputs, and refine final decisions. Early multi-agent frameworks primarily use natural language as the communication medium, where agents exchange explicit messages under predefined roles or protocols [14, 8, 2]. While effective, such communication is inherently constrained by the discreteness of text: when internal states are externalized as token sequences, uncertainty over alternatives and other unresolved information can be collapsed into a more determinate representation during transmission. This limitation has motivated increasing interest in richer communication channels that move beyond natural language and preserve more of the model's internal computation [20, 23]. 

Among these directions, LatentMAS is particularly appealing because it enables one agent to relay its key-value (KV) cache directly to another agent, allowing downstream reasoning to continue from internal states rather than from text alone [33]. However, this higher-fidelity communication comes at a substantial cost. Relaying full KV caches is memory- and bandwidth-intensive, and the cost grows quickly with the number of agents, rounds, and prompt tokens involved.

A natural solution is to compress the communicated KV states. Recent work on efficient LLM inference suggests that not all cached states are equally important. Methods such as StreamingLLM, $H_2O$ , and Scissorhands show that selective retention or eviction of KV states can reduce memory

content.text:
# LCGuard: Latent Communication Guard for Safe KV Sharing in Multi-Agent Systems

Sadia Asif $^{1}$ Mohammad Mohammadi Amiri $^{1}$ Momin Abbas $^{2}$ Prasanna Sattigeri $^{2}$ Karthikeyan Natesan Ramamurthy $^{2}$ 

<sup>1</sup>Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute <sup>2</sup>IBM Research

■ asifs@rpi.edu

## **Abstract**

Large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems increasingly rely on intermediate communication to coordinate complex tasks. While most existing systems communicate through natural language, recent work shows that latent communication, particularly through transformer key-value (KV) caches, can improve efficiency and preserve richer task-relevant information. However, KV caches also encode contextual inputs, intermediate reasoning states, and agent-specific information, creating an opaque channel through which sensitive content may propagate across agents without explicit textual disclosure. 

Empirical evaluations across multiple model families and multi-agent benchmarks show that LCGuard consistently reduces reconstruction-based leakage and attack success rates while maintaining competitive task performance compared to standard KV-sharing baselines.

# 1 Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in *multi-agent systems* (MAS), where multiple specialized agents collaborate through coordination, delegation, and intermediate information exchange to solve complex tasks [23, 40, 38, 18]. Existing systems predominantly rely on *text-based communication*, in which each agent serializes its internal state into natural language and downstream agents reinterpret that text to continue reasoning [47, 33]. While flexible and interpretable, this paradigm is inefficient and lossy: agents repeatedly decode, tokenize, and reconstruct semantic state across communication steps [11, 48].

### 2.2 Multi-agent Communication

Most LLM-based agent systems use natural language for communication (Li et al., 2023a; Wu et al., 2024; Chan et al., 2024). While natural language offers flexibility, it may also introduce potential information loss.

A recent attempt to address this issue, CI-PHER (Pham et al., 2024), replaces natural language tokens with probability-weighted token em-

beddings during agent communication, showing potential in multi-agent debate settings. However, this approach only leverages surface-level token probability distributions from the final output layer, overlooking deeper, more informative, and more valuable hidden representations.

Another approach (Ramesh and Li, 2025) attempts to directly transfer hidden states between agents, but is restricted to a unidirectional transfer, where hidden states from a text-reading agent are transferred to an output-generating agent. It does not support dynamic, interactive exchanges typical in multi-agent systems.

A multi-agent LLM system (MAS) consists of N LLM agents $\mathcal{A} = \{A_1, A_2, \dots, A_N\}$ , each equipped with a role-specific system prompt, optional tool access, and a communication channel. content.text:
#### 2.2.2 Communication Mechanisms

The effectiveness of MAS largely depends on how agents exchange information and coordinate actions. Communication methods in MAS have evolved from simple message passing to sophisticated protocols that balance expressiveness, efficiency, and interoperability.

- (1) Structured Output. This approach employs formats like JSON (Li et al., 2024e; Chen et al., 2025g), XML (Zhang et al., 2025b; Kong et al., 2025), and executable code (Roucher et al., 2025) for inter-agent communication. The explicit structure and well-defined parameters ensure high machine readability and interpretability, while standardised formats facilitate cross-platform collaboration (Chen et al., 2025g). These characteristics make structured communication ideal for applications demanding precision and efficiency, such as problem-solving and reasoning tasks. The compact information representation further enhances computational efficiency (Wang et al., 2024h).
- (2) Natural Language. 

Natural language communication preserves rich contextual and semantic details, making it particularly suitable for creative tasks, world simulation, and creative writing scenarios (Liu et al., 2025a). This expressiveness enables nuanced interactions that capture subtle meanings and intentions. However, it introduces challenges including ambiguity, potential misinterpretation, and reduced execution efficiency compared to structured formats (Guo et al., 2024c; Yang et al., 2025c; Kong et al., 2025).
- (3) Standardised Protocols. Recent advances have introduced specialised protocols designed to standardise MAS communication, creating more inclusive and interoperable agent ecosystems: A2A (LLC and Contributors) standardises horizontal communication through a structured, peer-to-peer task delegation model, enabling agents to collaborate on complex, long-running tasks while maintaining execution opacity.

#### 1 Introduction

Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed within Agentic AI systems, where they consume structured tool descriptions, interpret execution results, and emit tool invocations to accomplish user tasks. As these systems scale to more tools, longer descriptions, and richer result payloads, token consumption grows substantially. Because both inference cost and context-window limits are measured in tokens, the encoding of structured data is a direct determinant of system cost, energy efficiency, and feasibility.

In current tool-augmented pipelines, JSON is the default data format for tool schemas, invocations, and results (Bourhis et al., 2017), and LLMs interpret it effectively because of extensive exposure in their training corpora. 

JSON was, however, designed for application-to-application data interchange and not optimized for token efficiency, so its structural elements (quotation marks, commas, braces) impose substantial token overhead when consumed by LLMs. Recent work proposes token-optimized alternatives such as TOON (Token-Oriented Object Notation) (Schopplich, 2026; Lafalce, 2025) and TRON (Token Reduced Object Notation) (Huang, 2026), with initial results suggesting that LLMs can read TOON with minimal accuracy loss on isolated generation tasks (Masciari et al., 2026). ## 1 INTRODUCTION

LLM-based multi-agent systems have adopted natural language as their default communication medium [19]. Frameworks such as AutoGen [22], LangGraph [11], and CrewAI [1] enable developers to decompose complex tasks across specialized agents that collaborate through dialogue. While this linguistic flexibility lowers the barrier to multi-agent design, it introduces critical vulnerabilities: semantic drift, where meaning degrades across successive agent reinterpretations; hallucination propagation, where fabricated claims in one agent's output corrupt downstream reasoning; and computational waste, where verbose natural language exchanges consume tokens far in excess of their information content.

content.text:
Good — this maps to a very active (and surprisingly crowded) research area, so I did a literature pass before writing this up. Here's the honest critique, not a rubber-stamp.

## 1. Where this idea already exists in the literature

The core claim in your document — "LLMs think in vectors, agents needlessly serialize into English and reconstruct vectors again, so let's design a machine-oriented representation instead" — is not a hypothesis anymore. It's an active subfield with multiple 2025–2026 papers occupying almost exactly your framing:

**Latent-space communication (your "embedding/latent vector" candidate):**
- **Interlat** (Nov 2025) transmits an LLM's last hidden states directly between agents instead of natural language, with a learned compression step, and reports it beats fine-tuned chain-of-thought prompting and single-agent baselines by treating hidden states as a transmissible "mind" representation rather than downsampling them into tokens.
- **LatentMAS** (Princeton/UIUC/Stanford, Nov 2025) relays KV-cache state directly between agents so a receiving agent continues reasoning from internal state rather than re-reading text, and reports roughly 14.6% higher accuracy, 83.7% fewer tokens, and 4.3x faster inference versus text-based multi-agent baselines.
- **CIPHER** (Pham et al., 2024) already tried probability-weighted token embeddings for inter-agent debate, though a 2025 follow-up (State Delta Trajectory) notes it only uses surface-level output-layer distributions and misses richer hidden-state information.
- There's already a **survey paper** unifying this exact space: "Beyond tokens: a unified framework for latent communication in LLM-based multi-agent systems" (mid-2026), which formalizes the comparison between natural-language and latent communication channels as its core contribution.
- Compression follow-ons already exist too — a 2026 paper is specifically about compressing relayed KV-caches because relaying full KV caches is memory- and bandwidth-intensive and the cost grows quickly with agents, rounds, and prompt length.
- Security has already been raised as a problem: LCGuard exists because KV caches encode contextual inputs and reasoning state, creating an opaque channel through which sensitive content can leak across agents without explicit textual disclosure.

**Structured/symbolic communication (your "JSON / typed object / graph" candidates):**
- Structured formats like JSON, XML, and executable code are already an established category in multi-agent surveys, valued for machine-readability and cross-platform interoperability, and are described as ideal for problem-solving and reasoning tasks specifically because of their compact representation.
- A 2026 benchmark ("Notation Matters") goes further than plain JSON and tests token-optimized serializations (TOON, TRON) against JSON inside real agentic tool-calling pipelines involving tool discovery, multi-turn reasoning, and execution — this is essentially Stage 3–4 of your own methodology document, already executed by someone else.
- **G2CP** (AAMAS 2026) is a graph-grounded protocol built explicitly to fix the failure mode your module describes (semantic drift across paraphrasing), motivated by a worked example where one agent's "bearing failure" is reinterpreted by a second agent as a different bearing type, cascading into a wrong cost estimate — because natural language lacks the precision needed for reliable inter-agent reference.
- **EcoLANG** and others already explore agents autonomously inducing their own compact communication language rather than using English, citing prior work suggesting agents should be pushed toward structured languages like JSON, or fine-tuned specifically to improve inter-agent communication efficiency.

**Protocol-layer efforts (your "ABI/IR" framing):** MCP, A2A, ANP, Agora, and agents.json already exist as competing standardization efforts, with at least one comparative analysis noting that mature implementations already dynamically select between a known efficient protocol, a JSON structured-data fallback, and natural language as a last resort — i.e., the "hybrid representation" row in your own candidate table is already a shipped design pattern, not just a research idea.

**Verdict on novelty of the base framing:** the "Agent IR" idea, the CPU-ISA analogy, the compiler/LLVM-IR analogy, and the "state vs. data" distinction are all *good pedagogical framings*, but none of them are novel as research claims in mid-2026. If you present this module as "we're the first to ask whether agents should stop using English," reviewers with any currency in this area (this is a fast-moving space — several of these papers are from the last 60 days) will flag it immediately.

## 2. What's actually still open (the real gaps)

This doesn't mean the module is worthless — it means the contribution has to move up a level from "should agents use non-language representations" (answered: yes, repeatedly) to something sharper. Genuine gaps I can identify from what's out there:

1. **No standard benchmark suite exists yet for cross-paradigm comparison.** Every paper above benchmarks its own method against natural language, but almost none benchmark latent-vector methods against structured-symbolic methods against each other under identical tasks/models. Your Stage 3–4 (implement multiple methods under one harness, benchmark head-to-head) is a real gap — it's closer to a systematization/benchmarking contribution than a novel-method contribution.
2. **Verifiability and interpretability of latent channels remain unsolved.** Latent/KV-cache communication is efficient but opaque — you can't easily audit *why* an agent passed what it passed, and LCGuard shows it's already a security liability. A hybrid approach with a verifiable symbolic "audit trail" alongside a compressed latent fast-path is a more defensible novel angle than either extreme alone.
3. **Heterogeneous-model communication is barely explored.** Interlat tests cross-model latent transfer, but general symbolic/hybrid representations that work across different model families/vendors (which matters more in practice, since real deployments mix models) are underexplored.
4. **Confidence-aware and execution-aware state representations** (your Stage 7 list) are mentioned as future directions in multiple papers but rarely implemented end-to-end with a scheduler that acts on the confidence signal.

## 3. Feasibility assessment

- **Structured/symbolic track (JSON, typed objects, graphs):** fully feasible at your scale (student project, no special hardware). You can implement this with prompt-engineering + schema validation, no model access needed. Low risk, low compute cost.
- **Latent-vector track:** feasible but heavier. To transmit real hidden states or KV-caches you need white-box access to open-weight models (Llama/Qwen-class), not API-only models like Claude or GPT via standard endpoints — you cannot do this against a closed API. Compute cost is non-trivial (you're running two+ model instances and possibly fine-tuning a compression adapter, as Interlat does). This is realistic on a single decent GPU for small models (1B–8B) but not for large frontier models.
- **Fair benchmarking across both tracks** is the actual hard engineering problem: you need task suites where both a latent-capable and an API-only symbolic agent can be evaluated on identical inputs, which usually means picking open-weight models throughout so the comparison is apples-to-apples.

## 4. Where I'd push back on your document's framing specifically

- The CPU-ISA analogy is evocative but slightly misleading: CPU stages share a *fixed, hand-designed* ISA because correctness is provable and the state space is small. LLM "state" is high-dimensional, model-specific, and non-stationary across training runs — you can't just define an opcode table. This needs to be acknowledged explicitly, or a reviewer will call it out.
- "The information remains identical" across your Paris/France encodings example is not actually true for neural systems — converting from natural language to JSON to a graph to an embedding are *not* lossless round-trips in practice; each has different failure modes (JSON is more precise but not learned end-to-end; embeddings are compact but not interpretable and not consistent across checkpoints). Frame this as a trade-off space, not equivalent encodings of one Platonic "information," or your core research question becomes trivially false.
- Your research question ("minimal machine-oriented representation... with equal or better performance than natural language") is good, but as posed it's already been answered "yes" multiple times in 2025–2026 papers above. You need to add a constraint that makes it non-trivial again — e.g., "...under closed-model (API-only) conditions where hidden states aren't accessible" or "...while remaining human-auditable for safety-critical verification," since those are the parts nobody's nailed yet.

## 5. Recommended reposition

Given the field's current state, I'd steer the project toward:

**"A comparative benchmark of machine-oriented agent communication under realistic deployment constraints (API-only models, mixed model vendors, and required auditability), with a proposed hybrid symbolic-fast-path/verifiable-audit-trail protocol."**

This keeps your Stages 1–6 (survey, reproduce, benchmark existing methods) exactly as planned — that part is legitimately valuable and underdone as a *unified* benchmark, even though individual methods exist. It reframes Stage 7's novel contribution toward the two gaps that are real: (a) cross-vendor/API-only feasibility, and (b) verifiability, rather than "yet another latent communication scheme," which is now a crowded lane.

**Practical roadmap:**
1. Literature/benchmark survey (you're most of the way there — add the papers above to your literature DB).
2. Reproduce: natural language, JSON/typed-object, one symbolic graph method, and (if you have open-weight model access) one latent method as a stretch goal.
3. Common benchmark: multi-agent task suite (e.g., multi-hop QA, code review pipeline, or literature-review pipeline — convenient, since you already have ResearchGap AI's agent architecture to reuse as a testbed) with metrics: token count, latency, task accuracy, and a *new* metric — auditability (can a human reconstruct why the decision was made from the transmitted state, scored via a rubric or secondary LLM judge).
4. Propose the hybrid protocol only after the benchmark exposes where symbolic methods fail and where latent/compressed methods win.
5. Write it up positioned as a systematization/benchmarking paper (which is a legitimate, publishable venue-appropriate contribution — think AAMAS/workshop-tier) rather than oversold as "the first machine communication protocol for agents," which won't survive a related-work section.

## 6. Bottom line on your explicit ask

- **Novel as originally framed:** No — multiple groups (Princeton/UIUC/Stanford, several AAMAS 2026 submissions, IETF drafts) are actively publishing on exactly this question right now.
- **Novel if repositioned around benchmarking + API-only feasibility + auditability:** Yes, plausibly — those are real, currently-unaddressed gaps.
- **Technically feasible for you:** Yes for the symbolic/structured track at full depth; latent-vector track is feasible only with open-weight models and added compute/engineering cost.
- **Impactful:** Moderate — a rigorous cross-paradigm benchmark would be genuinely citable and useful even without a flashy new method, because right now every paper benchmarks only against natural language, not against each other.

Want me to help draft the revised research question and Stage 1 literature database entries reflecting these papers, so your existing methodology doc stays intact but the framing gets corrected before you go further?

To tackle this, we propose OSC (Orchestrating Cognitive Synergy), an end-to-end, knowledge-aware adaptive collaboration framework. OSC serves as an intermediate layer, enhancing linguistic interactions among selected experts without replacing expert In its "inter-expert selection or aggregation. collaborative communication" phase, each agent $e_i$ uses a dynamically learned Collaborator Knowledge Model $(CKM_i(e_i \mid Q, H_t))$ to track collaborators' cognitive states (knowledge, reasoning, task understanding via $H_t$ ). CKM parameters ( $\theta_{\text{CKM}}, \theta_{\text{update}}$ ), initially pretrained, are fine-tuned end-to-end within OSC's RL loop, tailoring them for effective collaboration. A learnable cognitive gap analysis module $(G_{i,j})$ informs a policy $\pi_{\mathrm{comm}}$ , which dynamically shapes communication behavior $M_{i\to j}$ (content, style, objectives; $\Phi_i^{(t)}$ as $e_i$ 's state). 

OSC introduces a structured linguistic interaction phase, transforming selected expert agents from parallel workers into a cohesive, intelligent team. This phase features dynamically learned models of agents' cognitive states and adaptive communication policies, fine-tuned end-to-end. These enable agents to perceive, reason, and respond to evolving team knowledge and intentions. Through integrated learning, agents refine solutions, resolve conflicts, and reach robust consensus before final answer aggregation, guided by a reinforcement-learned communication policy, $\pi_{\text{comm}}$ (see Section 3.4).

To overcome this challenge, we present the Dynamic Size Message Scheduling (DSMS) method, which introduces a finer-grained approach to scheduling by considering the actual size of the information to be exchanged. Our contribution lies in adaptively adjusting message sizes using Fourier transform-based compression techniques, enabling agents to tailor their messages to match the allocated bandwidth while striking a balance between information loss and transmission efficiency. Receiving agents can reliably decompress the messages using the inverse Fourier transform. Experimental results demonstrate that DSMS significantly improves performance in multi-agent cooperative tasks by optimizing the utilization of bandwidth and effectively balancing information value.

Good instinct to push back — and the search confirms your worry is justified in a *different* direction than I first pointed you. "Adaptive representation selection" is now also crowded: ProtocolRouter picks a whole protocol per scenario, AMAS and DynaSwarm use RL to pick agent topology per query, OSC uses an RL-trained "Collaborator Knowledge Model" to shape communication style dynamically, and Agent Q-Mix casts communication choice as a learned MARL policy. So "let the system learn/choose the best format dynamically" is also already someone's PhD-in-progress, and all of them need RL training loops and infrastructure you don't have time or GPU budget for in a semester.

Here's the actual gap I see after this second pass: **every one of these systems (RL routers, latent comm, structured comm) treats correctness/consistency checking as something the LLM itself is trusted to do, or something an RL reward signal handles implicitly.** None of them bring in classical KRR machinery — actual belief revision, defeasible reasoning, or formal consistency checking — as an explicit, inspectable layer sitting between agents. G2CP gets close (graph grounding to fix ambiguity) but it's about referential precision, not about what happens when Agent B receives something that *contradicts* what it already believes.

## The pivot: a semantic firewall for multi-agent systems, built on classical belief revision

**Idea:** every inter-agent message gets converted into a structured belief object (claim + evidence + confidence + source), and a lightweight reasoning layer — built on actual KR theory (AGM belief revision, or a simpler defeasible-logic ruleset) — sits between agents and:

1. **Checks internal consistency** of an incoming belief against the receiving agent's current belief state before it's accepted.
2. **Flags or resolves contradictions** using a formal revision policy (e.g., prefer higher-confidence/more-recent/better-sourced evidence — this is literally what AGM belief revision postulates formalize) instead of just letting the LLM silently overwrite or hallucinate around it.
3. **Produces an audit trail** — a human-readable log of every belief accepted, rejected, or revised and *why*, which is the part that's genuinely missing from every method I found (latent methods are opaque by construction; RL routers optimize a reward, not an explainable rule).

This is why it's actually KRR rather than "systems engineering with a fancy name": belief revision, consistency maintenance, and defeasible reasoning are classical, well-theorized KR topics (Alchourrón-Gärdenfors-Makinson, argumentation frameworks, truth maintenance systems) — you're applying 1980s-90s symbolic AI theory to a very 2026 problem (LLM agents hallucinating and silently contradicting each other across a pipeline). That combination — "old KR machinery bolted onto new LLM multi-agent failure modes" — is genuinely thin in the current literature, which is dominated by learned/RL/neural approaches on one side and pure efficiency/serialization work on the other.

## Why this fixes your actual constraints

- **Niche and not cliché:** nobody's pitch right now is "belief revision as a runtime firewall for LLM agents" — it's a specific, defensible angle, not "faster agent chat."
- **Feasible without heavy infra:** no RL training, no need for open-weight model internals. A rule engine or even a simple constraint checker (Python + a small logic library, or a lightweight Datalog/answer-set solver like Clingo) is enough. Works fine against Claude/GPT APIs.
- **Demoable at every review**, because it's a real running component, not a training pipeline you wait on:
  - **Review 1:** the belief schema + a working 2-agent demo where you deliberately inject a contradiction (e.g., two sources disagree) and show the firewall catching it and logging why, versus the same scenario in plain NL where the contradiction silently corrupts downstream output. This before/after is a strong, visual, "ticks people's brains" demo.
  - **Review 2:** scaled onto your actual ResearchGap AI pipeline (multiple agents, real literature-review task), plus the revision policy (how the firewall decides which belief wins when two agents disagree), plus first benchmark numbers (rate of caught contradictions, hallucination propagation reduction vs. no-firewall baseline).
  - **Final:** packaged as a reusable middleware library + full benchmark write-up comparing NL / plain-JSON / your firewall-guarded protocol on hallucination-propagation rate, contradiction-catch rate, token/latency overhead, and task accuracy.
- **Resume line writes itself:** "Designed and implemented a belief-revision-based verification layer for multi-agent LLM systems that detects and resolves contradictory information before it propagates downstream — reducing hallucination cascades by X%." That's specific, technical, and not something every other CS student's resume also says this cycle.

## One honest risk to flag

Belief revision theory (AGM) was built for propositional/first-order logic, not for the fuzzy, natural-language-derived claims LLMs produce. You'll need to simplify — e.g., represent each belief as a `(claim, confidence, source, timestamp)` tuple rather than full first-order formulas, and use a simplified revision rule (confidence + recency + source-reliability weighting) rather than textbook AGM contraction/expansion operators. That's a legitimate, defensible simplification for a bachelor's-level project, but you should state it explicitly as a scoping decision in your report rather than pretend you've implemented full AGM — a professor who knows KR will ask, and "we adapted AGM's core postulates to a tractable tuple-based approximation, here's why" is a much stronger answer than getting caught overclaiming.

## The project: Interpretability-Guided Behavior Editing via Sparse Autoencoders

**Core idea:** Train a sparse autoencoder (SAE) on the internal activations of a small open-weight LLM to decompose its "thinking" into individually interpretable features, then use those features as surgical handles to detect and correct a specific unwanted behavior — factual errors, hallucinations, or a targeted concept — without retraining the model.

**Why this isn't generic:** almost no undergrad projects touch mechanistic interpretability — it's dominated by a handful of labs (Anthropic, DeepMind, EleutherAI) and a small research community. Your peers are building RAG pipelines and agent orchestrators; you'd be doing something that looks like it belongs in an alignment/interpretability team's portfolio.

**Honest caveat (I checked, so you don't get blindsided in a viva):** this is an *active* research area, not virgin territory — there's a real 2025–2026 line of work on this (SAE-based unlearning, hallucination-feature suppression, concept erasure, reasoning-steering). Importantly, one well-known paper, **AxBench**, found that simple baselines (like mean-difference activation steering) often beat SAE-based steering. That's not a reason to avoid the project — it's your built-in research question: **"When does the extra machinery of SAEs actually earn its keep over a dumb linear baseline, for a specific editing task?"** That framing makes your project a rigorous comparative study rather than "I tried SAEs, cool graphs," which is exactly the kind of honest, evidence-driven framing that survives a professor's scrutiny.

### Why it fits your constraints
- **Compute-feasible:** small models (GPT-2-small/medium, Pythia-410M, or Llama-3.2-1B) run fine on a free-tier Colab/Kaggle GPU. You don't need a cluster.
- **Mix of train + orchestrate:** you train the SAE yourself (the "train" part) while orchestrating an existing pretrained LLM and libraries like TransformerLens and SAELens (the "orchestrate" part) — exactly the split you asked for.
- **Ambitious but boundable:** the scope naturally grows in layers, so you're never stuck waiting on one giant training run.

- Train (or fine-tune an existing) SAE on residual-stream activations.
- Validate quality: reconstruction loss, sparsity, and — the fun demo part — a feature dashboard showing "here are 10 features and the text snippets that light each one up," some of which will visibly correspond to real human concepts.
- Demo: a live, browsable interface (even a simple Streamlit app, which you've already got experience with from StudyMind) showing interpretable features on real text.

**Review 2 — Control**
- Build intervention machinery: ablate/amplify specific features during generation.
- Implement the baseline you're benchmarking against (mean-difference / contrastive activation addition — much simpler, a few dozen lines).
- Demo: side-by-side generations — same prompt, unmodified model vs. SAE-steered vs. baseline-steered — for 2–3 target behaviors (e.g., suppress a specific factual error, reduce a specific unwanted tone).

Generalization means that your knowledge of a fact is robust to changes in wording and context. After learning the Eiffel Tower is in Rome, then you should also know that visiting it will require travel to Rome. Our new dataset CounterFact includes thousands of counterfactuals along with text that allows quantitative testing of specificity and generalization when learning a counterfactual. Above are the results of an experiment that uses CounterFact to confirm the distinction between knowing and saying parameters in GPT-2 XL. ROME, which edits the early causal site (a), achieves excellent efficacy (measured by performance on the counterfactual prompt itself), specificity (performance on neighborhood subjects not supposed to change), and generalization (performance on paraphrases). By contrast, if we modify the attention mechanism at the later site (b), the model achieves fair efficacy and specificity but completely fails to generalize.



At (a) in in the figure, a single direct statement of a counterfactual is posed, and it is used to compute a rank-one parameter change in a single MLP module. Despite the simplicity of the change, results shown at (b) show that for a more complex prompt about travel from Berlin, the model treats the Eiffel tower as if it is in Rome; similarly in (c) when asked about nearby sites, the model suggests places in Rome before explicitly mentioning Rome. Changes in predictions in such different contexts is evidence that change generalizes: the model has not merely learned to parrot the exact sequence of words in the counterfactual, but it also applies the new knowledge in sentences that are very different from the original example. To identify decisive computations, we introduce a method called Causal Tracing. By isolating the causal effect of individual states within the network while processing a factual statement, we can trace the path followed by information through the network.

input.file_text:
# FeatureScalpel: Interpretability-Guided Behavior Editing in Small Language Models

### A Comparative Study of Sparse-Autoencoder-Based Model Editing Against Classical Baselines

---

## 1. Field

**Primary field:** Mechanistic Interpretability (a subfield of Deep Learning / Trustworthy & Explainable AI)
**Secondary fields touched:** Knowledge Editing, Representation Engineering, Model Behavior Control

Mechanistic interpretability studies the internal computations of neural networks well enough to explain, predict, and — as in this project — *causally intervene on* their behavior, rather than treating them as black boxes probed only from the outside (prompting, output analysis). This project sits at the intersection of interpretability research and the more applied "knowledge editing" literature, which asks: can we surgically fix a specific belief or behavior in a trained model without retraining it?

---

## 2. Abstract

Large language models frequently encode outdated, incorrect, or undesirable factual associations (e.g. "the Eiffel Tower is in Rome" after a factual drift, or a systematic hallucination pattern). Existing fixes are blunt: full retraining is expensive, and prompting-based fixes don't generalize. A parallel line of research — sparse autoencoders (SAEs) — has shown that a language model's internal activations can be decomposed into a much larger set of sparse, individually interpretable "features," each corresponding to a recognizable human concept. This project investigates whether such SAE-derived features can be used as precise, inspectable levers to detect and correct factual/behavioral errors in a small open-weight language model, and — critically — whether this approach earns its added complexity over much simpler activation-steering baselines (e.g. mean-difference steering), a question raised directly by recent literature (Wu et al., "AxBench," 2025) that found SAEs often underperform naive baselines for steering tasks.

The project trains an SAE on a small open-weight LLM, builds an intervention pipeline that uses discovered features to edit specific factual associations, and rigorously benchmarks this against (a) simple activation-steering baselines and (b) the classical weight-editing literature (ROME, MEMIT) on a curated factual-editing benchmark, reporting efficacy, generalization, and specificity — the three standard axes of the model-editing literature (Meng et al., 2022). The deliverable is both a research-style comparative evaluation and a working, demonstrable tool: an interactive feature dashboard plus a live "before/after" editing demo.

---

## 3. Why This Matters (Motivation / Usefulness)

- **Practical:** Retraining a model to fix one wrong fact or one bad behavioral tendency is wasteful and can introduce new regressions. A method that edits a specific belief while leaving everything else untouched has direct utility for model maintenance, safety patching, and personalization.
- **Scientific:** SAEs are one of the most actively studied interpretability tools of 2024–2026, but most of the excitement has focused on *finding* interpretable features. Comparatively little undergraduate-accessible work rigorously asks whether those features are *useful* for a concrete downstream task, compared to much cheaper alternatives. This project produces an honest answer for one task (factual editing), rather than an SAE showcase.
- **Career relevance:** Interpretability and model-editing skills are directly relevant to AI safety/alignment research groups (Anthropic, DeepMind, EleutherAI, academic labs) and are still rare among undergraduate portfolios, unlike agent/RAG projects.

---

## 4. Novelty Check — What Already Exists (Literature Review)

I checked this space deliberately before finalizing the plan, because the goal is a real contribution, not a rediscovery. Summary of what already exists and where this project sits relative to it:

### 4.1 Classical (non-interpretability) model editing
- **ROME** (Meng et al., NeurIPS 2022, *"Locating and Editing Factual Associations in GPT"*) showed that factual associations are localized in mid-layer MLP modules and can be edited via a rank-one weight update, introducing the **CounterFact** benchmark (efficacy / generalization / specificity) that this project reuses.
- **MEMIT** extends ROME to batch-edit thousands of facts at once.
- Follow-up work (**CounterFact+**, Hoelscher-Obermaier et al.) showed ROME/MEMIT edits have real side effects on unrelated ("neighborhood") facts that the original CounterFact benchmark under-detects — an important methodological lesson this project incorporates by using a specificity-sensitive evaluation, not just the original metric.
- These methods edit **weights directly** using causal tracing, not interpretable features. This project asks a different question: can a *feature-based* (SAE) approach match or beat them while being more inspectable and requiring no weight surgery calculus?

### 4.2 SAE-based steering, editing, and unlearning (2024–2026)
This is an active, fast-moving area — this project is a contribution *within* it, not a rediscovery of it:
- **SAFE** (Abdaljalil et al., 2025) suppresses hallucination-associated SAE features to raise factual accuracy in open-domain QA.
- **SALVE** (Flovik, 2025) performs weight-space edits guided by sparse features for precise concept suppression/enhancement.
- **SASFT** (ICLR 2026) uses SAE-guided fine-tuning for a related but distinct goal (cross-lingual behavior control).
- Farrell, Lau & Conmy (2024) and Gandikota et al. (2025) explore SAE-based **unlearning**/concept erasure specifically.
- **AxBench** (Wu et al., 2025) is the critical counter-finding: across several steering tasks, simple supervised baselines (e.g. difference-of-means steering) matched or beat SAE-based steering, despite SAEs being more expensive to train. This is the single most important paper for keeping this project honest — it directly motivates the comparative (not celebratory) framing below.
- **SAE-Steering** (Fang et al., 2026) shows SAE features can redirect reasoning-model behavior with a measured accuracy gain over baselines specifically for *reasoning strategy* control — evidence that SAE-based control *can* win in the right setting, which supports investigating whether factual-editing is such a setting.

**Where this project fits:** Nearly all the above papers pick one method and show it works on their chosen task. This project explicitly reproduces a simple baseline, a classical weight-editing baseline (ROME, at least on the small models it's tractable for), and an SAE-based method, on the *same* curated benchmark, and reports where each wins and loses — a systematic three-way comparison focused specifically on factual editing, which none of the papers above provide together. This is the concrete, defensible novelty claim: **not "SAEs are cool," but "here is rigorous evidence for when the extra SAE machinery is or isn't worth it for factual editing on a small model."**

### 4.3 Tooling landscape (confirms feasibility, not a gap — just infrastructure)
- **TransformerLens** (Nanda et al.) — standard library for extracting and hooking into activations of open-weight transformer models.
- **SAELens** (Bloom et al.) — standard library for training and loading SAEs, with pretrained SAEs available for models like GPT-2-small via community hubs (e.g. Neuronpedia).
- Using these means the "plumbing" is already solved; your engineering effort goes into the actual research question, not reinventing activation hooks.

---

## 5. Core Research Questions

1. Can SAE-derived features be used to reliably detect when a small LLM is about to state a specific incorrect fact?
2. Can ablating/steering along those features correct the output, and does the correction generalize across paraphrasings of the same fact (the "generalization" axis from CounterFact)?
3. Does this correction stay *specific* — i.e., does it avoid corrupting unrelated, nearby facts (the well-documented failure mode of ROME/MEMIT per CounterFact+)?
4. How does SAE-based editing compare, on the same benchmark, to (a) a simple mean-difference activation-steering baseline and (b) classical weight-editing (ROME), on efficacy, generalization, specificity, and implementation cost?

---

## 6. System Architecture

```
                         ┌─────────────────────────────┐
                         │   Small Open-Weight LLM      │
                         │ (GPT-2-small/medium, or      │
                         │  Pythia-410M / Llama-3.2-1B) │
                         └──────────────┬───────────────┘
                                        │ activations (residual stream)
                                        ▼
                         ┌─────────────────────────────┐
                         │  Activation Extraction Layer │
                         │      (TransformerLens)       │
                         └──────────────┬───────────────┘
                                        │
                     ┌──────────────────┼───────────────────┐
                     ▼                                      ▼
        ┌─────────────────────────┐            ┌─────────────────────────┐
        │   Sparse Autoencoder    │            │  Baseline: Mean-Diff /  │
        │   (trained via SAELens) │            │  Contrastive Activation │
        │  → sparse feature space │            │  Addition (CAA) vector │
        └───────────┬─────────────┘            └────────────┬────────────┘
                     │ feature activations                   │ steering vector
                     ▼                                        ▼
        ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
        │             Intervention / Editing Engine                     │
        │  - Feature search: find feature(s) correlated with a target   │
        │    fact/behavior                                              │
        │  - Ablation / amplification during generation                 │
        │  - (Optional) weight-space edit guided by feature direction   │
        └───────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────┘
                                     │
                                     ▼
                     ┌───────────────────────────────┐
                     │   Evaluation Harness           │
                     │  - Efficacy / Generalization /│
                     │    Specificity on CounterFact  │
                     │    subset                      │
                     │  - Compared against ROME       │
                     │    (classical weight-edit)     │
                     └───────────────────────────────┘
                                     │
                                     ▼
                     ┌───────────────────────────────┐
                     │  Interactive Demo Layer        │
                     │  - Feature dashboard (Streamlit)│
                     │  - Live before/after generation │
                     │    comparison                  │
                     └───────────────────────────────┘
```

---

## 7. Technical Approach

### 7.1 Model & data choice
- **Model:** GPT-2-small/medium (124M/355M) for the core pipeline (pretrained SAEs already exist for GPT-2-small via community sources, reducing risk), with a stretch goal of repeating key experiments on Pythia-410M or Llama-3.2-1B if time and compute allow, to show the method isn't a one-model fluke.
- **Facts dataset:** a curated subset (150–300 records) of the CounterFact dataset (Meng et al., 2022), supplemented with a small hand-built set of "neighborhood" prompts per fact for specificity testing (following the lesson from CounterFact+).

### 7.2 Stage A — SAE training and validation
- Extract residual-stream activations at 2–3 candidate layers.
- Train an SAE (start with a standard ReLU SAE; JumpReLU as a stretch goal per Rajamanoharan et al., 2024, for better reconstruction fidelity).
- Validate: reconstruction loss, L0 sparsity, and manual/auto-interpretation of top-activating features (can reuse LLM-based auto-interpretation, i.e. asking an LLM to summarize what a feature seems to represent from its top activating examples).

### 7.3 Stage B — Feature-guided intervention
- Given a target fact (e.g. "Eiffel Tower → Rome" counterfactual), locate candidate features correlated with the correct/incorrect answer via activation differencing.
- Build an ablation/steering intervention that suppresses or amplifies these features during generation.
- Build the baseline in parallel: a simple difference-of-means steering vector for the same fact, computed directly from activations (no SAE needed) — this is the AxBench-style baseline this project is explicitly built to compare against.

### 7.4 Stage C — Benchmarking
- Run all three methods (SAE-feature edit, mean-diff/CAA baseline, and ROME as the classical weight-edit reference — feasible on GPT-2-small/medium using the original ROME codebase) on the same curated fact set.
- Metrics, following Meng et al. (2022) and the CounterFact+ refinement:
  - **Efficacy:** does the edited model now prefer the target answer over the original?
  - **Generalization:** does the edit hold under paraphrased prompts?
  - **Specificity:** do nearby, unrelated facts stay correct (measured both by the original neighborhood score and, if time allows, the KL-divergence-based specificity metric from CounterFact+)?
  - **Cost:** wall-clock time and engineering complexity per method — this is the practical angle that makes the comparison meaningful, not just academic.

### 7.5 Stage D — Demo layer
- Streamlit dashboard: browse SAE features with their top-activating text examples.
- Live "before/after" generation comparison for a handful of curated example edits, for both the SAE method and the baseline, side by side.

---

## 8. Tools & Technology Stack

| Component | Tool |
|---|---|
| Activation access / hooking | TransformerLens |
| SAE training/loading | SAELens (+ pretrained GPT-2-small SAEs from Neuronpedia/community hub as a fallback/reference) |
| Classical weight-editing baseline | ROME reference implementation (kmeng01/rome) |
| Model | GPT-2-small/medium (core), Pythia-410M or Llama-3.2-1B (stretch) |
| Compute | Free-tier Colab/Kaggle T4 GPU is sufficient for all of the above at this model scale; no multi-GPU or large-cluster requirement |
| Demo | Streamlit (already familiar from prior project experience) |
| Dataset | CounterFact (Meng et al., 2022) subset + hand-curated neighborhood prompts |

---

## 9. Feasibility Assessment

- **Compute:** Fully feasible on a single free-tier GPU. SAE training on residual-stream activations of a 124M–410M-parameter model, over a few thousand text samples, typically completes in hours, not days. ROME edits on GPT-2-scale models are near-instant (a rank-one update per fact).
- **Data availability:** CounterFact is public and directly downloadable; no licensing or access barriers (unlike your previous digital-twin project's classified-data problem — this sidesteps that entirely).
- **Tooling maturity:** TransformerLens, SAELens, and the ROME codebase are all mature, documented, actively maintained open-source libraries with existing tutorials — the "plumbing" risk is low.
- **Time budget:** the three-stage split (discover → intervene → benchmark) maps cleanly onto a three-review semester structure, each stage producing an independently demoable artifact, so there's no single point where you're "waiting for training to finish" with nothing to show.
- **Main risk:** feature interpretability and steering effectiveness are known to be inconsistent across facts and layers in the literature (this is a known open problem, not a sign you're doing something wrong) — mitigate by choosing several candidate facts up front and reporting honestly on both successes and failures, which is itself valid research signal per the evaluation questions above.

---

## 10. Development Roadmap (Three-Review Structure)

**Review 1 — Discovery (interpretability foundation)**
- Activation extraction pipeline working end-to-end.
- SAE trained (or pretrained SAE adapted) with validated reconstruction quality.
- Feature dashboard demo: browsable, interpretable features with real text examples.

**Review 2 — Control (intervention pipeline)**
- Feature-guided ablation/steering implemented.
- Mean-diff/CAA baseline implemented in parallel.
- Live demo: before/after generation for 2–3 target facts/behaviors, both methods side by side.

**Final Review — Rigorous comparison + packaged tool**
- ROME baseline integrated for the classical-editing comparison.
- Full benchmark run across all three methods on the curated CounterFact subset: efficacy, generalization, specificity, cost.
- Packaged demo (dashboard + live editing tool) plus a written comparative analysis of when each method wins.

---

## 11. Risks & Mitigations

| Risk | Mitigation |
|---|---|
| SAE features aren't cleanly interpretable for chosen facts | Select several candidate facts early; report both successes and failures — a null result on some facts is legitimate and expected given AxBench's findings |
| Steering degrades general model quality (not just the target fact) | Include a small held-out "general capability" check (e.g. perplexity on unrelated text) alongside specificity metrics |
| ROME integration is fiddly on non-GPT-2 models | Keep ROME comparison scoped to GPT-2-small/medium, where the reference implementation is well-tested; treat Pythia/Llama as stretch-only |
| Scope creep (trying to cover too many facts/behaviors) | Fix a small curated benchmark size (150–300 facts) up front rather than expanding indefinitely |

---

## 12. Expected Contributions / Deliverables

1. A working SAE-based feature-discovery and dashboard tool for a small open-weight LLM.
2. A feature-guided editing/steering pipeline.
3. A rigorous three-way comparison (SAE-feature editing vs. simple activation steering vs. classical weight editing) on a factual-editing benchmark, with honest reporting of trade-offs — the main research contribution.
4. A packaged, demoable interactive tool suitable for a final-review presentation.

---

## 13. Possible Extensions (if ahead of schedule)

- Repeat the full pipeline on a second model family (Pythia or Llama-3.2) to test whether conclusions transfer across architectures.
- Extend from single-fact edits to small batches (MEMIT-style), testing whether the SAE approach scales differently than weight-editing as edit count grows.
- Explore JumpReLU SAEs (Rajamanoharan et al., 2024) instead of standard ReLU SAEs for improved reconstruction fidelity, if reconstruction quality is a bottleneck.

---

## 14. Key References

- Meng, K. et al. (2022). *Locating and Editing Factual Associations in GPT* (ROME; introduces CounterFact). NeurIPS 2022.
- Meng, K. et al. (2023). *Mass-Editing Memory in a Transformer* (MEMIT).
- Hoelscher-Obermaier, J. et al. *Detecting Edit Failures in Large Language Models: An Improved Specificity Benchmark* (CounterFact+).
- Wu, Z., Arora, A., Geiger, A. et al. (2025). *AxBench: Steering LLMs? Even Simple Baselines Outperform Sparse Autoencoders.*
- Abdaljalil, S. et al. (2025). *SAFE: SAE-driven hallucination feature suppression for open-domain QA.*
- Flovik (2025). *SALVE: Sparse Autoencoder-Latent Vector Editing for Mechanistic Control of Neural Networks.*
- Farrell, E., Lau, Y.-T., Conmy, A. (2024). *Applying Sparse Autoencoders to Unlearn Knowledge in Language Models.*
- Gandikota, R. et al. (2025). *Erasing Conceptual Knowledge from Language Models.*
- Fang, Y. et al. (2026). *Controllable LLM Reasoning via Sparse Autoencoder-Based Steering.*
- Rajamanoharan, S. et al. (2024). *Jumping Ahead: Improving Reconstruction Fidelity with JumpReLU Sparse Autoencoders.*
- SASFT (2026), ICLR conference paper on SAE-guided fine-tuning for cross-lingual behavior control.
- Bloom, J., Chanin, D. et al. — SAELens library documentation.
- Nanda, N. et al. — TransformerLens library documentation.

---

*Prepared as a semester main-project proposal. All prior-art claims above are based on a targeted literature check conducted alongside this proposal; recommend re-verifying key citations directly (arXiv/OpenReview links) before including them in a formal submitted report.*
